health.button.title: {what}: {status}

health.copyHint: Copy this request and paste it into {app}, opened in your project folder. It explains what to change and asks before anything risky.
health.intro.code: We looked for keys left in the code or sent to the browser, data and parts of your app anyone on the internet can reach (Supabase tables, Firebase rules, Stripe webhooks, endpoints), leftover files and files too big to edit safely. It’s a quick check, not a security audit.
health.intro.plan: We checked the plan for parts anyone on the internet could use, decisions the PRD leaves open, and pieces nothing connects to. Settling these now is cheaper than after it’s built.
health.calm.code: Nothing stood out. This is a quick automatic check, not a full security review.
health.calm.plan: Nothing stood out. This is a quick automatic check, not a full design review.

health.rls.title.one: Anyone can read and change your {table} table
health.rls.title.other: Anyone can read and change {n} of your database tables
health.rls.detail.one: Your app talks to Supabase with a public key that every visitor’s browser has. Row-level security is what stops one person from reading or changing someone else’s rows, and it’s off for the {table} table. Without it, anyone can use that key to read, change or delete every row. If your app only reaches the database from its own server, the risk is lower, but switching it on is still the safe default.
health.rls.detail.other: Your app talks to Supabase with a public key that every visitor’s browser has. Row-level security is what stops one person from reading or changing someone else’s rows, and it’s off for {tables}. Without it, anyone can use that key to read, change or delete every row in them. If your app only reaches the database from its own server, the risk is lower, but switching it on is still the safe default.

health.open-policy.title.other: {n} database rules let anyone change your data
health.open-policy.detail.one: The rule “{policy}” lets anyone{signedOut} {rows}. If a table is a public form (like a waitlist or contact form), letting anyone add rows is fine; otherwise limit it to signed-in users and their own rows.
health.open-policy.detail.other: These rules let anyone{signedOut} add, change or delete rows in {tables}. If a table is a public form (like a waitlist or contact form), letting anyone add rows is fine; otherwise limit it to signed-in users and their own rows.
health.open-policy.signedOut: , even people who aren’t signed in,
health.open-policy.rows.all: add, change and delete rows in {table}
health.firebase-rules.until.title: Your Firebase {service} is open to anyone until {date}
health.firebase-rules.until.detail.files: {file} still has Firebase’s “test mode” rules: anyone can read and change every file until {date}, without signing in or using your app. After that date every request is refused and the app stops working, so replace them with real rules rather than moving the date.
health.firebase-rules.until.detail.data: {file} still has Firebase’s “test mode” rules: anyone can read and change everything until {date}, without signing in or using your app. After that date every request is refused and the app stops working, so replace them with real rules rather than moving the date.
health.firebase-rules.writes.title.files: Anyone can upload, replace or delete your Firebase files
health.firebase-rules.writes.title.data: Anyone can change or delete your Firebase {service} data
health.firebase-rules.writes.detail.file: A rule in {file} (line {n}, at {where}) lets anyone, signed in or not, upload, replace or delete files. Your app’s Firebase settings are in every visitor’s browser, so anyone can use them to reach your {service} directly, without going through your app.
health.firebase-rules.writes.detail.data: A rule in {file} (line {n}, at {where}) lets anyone, signed in or not, add, change or delete data. Your app’s Firebase settings are in every visitor’s browser, so anyone can use them to reach your {service} directly, without going through your app.
health.firebase-rules.reads.title: Anyone can read everything in your Firebase {service}
health.firebase-rules.reads.detail.files: A rule in {file} (line {n}) lets anyone read every file, including data that may belong to your users. If everything there is meant to be public, that’s fine; otherwise it needs a sign-in check.
health.firebase-rules.reads.detail.data: A rule in {file} (line {n}) lets anyone read every record, including data that may belong to your users. If everything there is meant to be public, that’s fine; otherwise it needs a sign-in check.
health.firebase-rules.partial.title: Anyone can change part of your Firebase {service}
health.firebase-rules.partial.detail.add: A rule in {file} (line {n}) lets anyone add to {where} without signing in. If that’s a public form (like a waitlist or contact form), that can be fine; otherwise it needs a sign-in check.
health.firebase-rules.partial.detail.cha: A rule in {file} (line {n}) lets anyone change {where} without signing in. If that’s a public form (like a waitlist or contact form), that can be fine; otherwise it needs a sign-in check.
health.firebase-rules.expired.title: Your Firebase {service} test-mode rules ran out on {date}
health.firebase-rules.expired.detail: {file} has Firebase’s “test mode” rules, which stopped allowing access on {date}. Every read and write is now refused, so the parts of the app that use {service} won’t work. Replace them with real rules instead of moving the date, which would open everything to anyone again.
health.stripe-webhook.title: Anyone could fake a Stripe payment in {name}
health.stripe-webhook.detail: {file} acts on Stripe events (like “{event}”) without checking Stripe’s signature, so anyone who finds the address can send a fake “payment succeeded” message and get orders, credits or a subscription for free. Stripe signs every real event; checking that signature takes a few lines.
health.stripe-webhook.note.route: Receives Stripe events without checking they’re real
health.stripe-webhook.note.file: line {n}: handles {events} without checking Stripe’s signature
health.cors.title.credentials: Any website could act as your signed-in users
health.cors.title.plain: Any website can call your server from a visitor’s browser
health.cors.detail.credentials: {file} lets any website call this server from a visitor’s browser and send along their login cookies. So a site a signed-in user happens to visit could quietly read their data or act as them. Allow only your own app’s address instead.
health.cors.detail.plain: {files} tell browsers that any website may call this server. That’s fine for a public API that doesn’t use login cookies (for example one that checks a token in the Authorization header); otherwise, allow only your own app’s address.
health.cors.how.header-echo: Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the caller’s origin

health.misplaced-guard.detail.other: On {endpoints} the login check (@{guard}) is written above the route line instead of below it. Flask only sees what's below, so they are open to anyone even though they look protected.

health.plan-no-access.note: Who may use this isn’t decided
health.plan-question.detail: The PRD doesn’t answer this, and the answer changes what gets built. Decide it before building the parts it touches.
health.plan-unused-endpoints.title.one: Nothing in the plan uses one endpoint
health.plan-unused-endpoints.title.other: Nothing in the plan uses {n} endpoints
health.plan-unused-endpoints.detail.one: No planned page or service calls it. Either a screen that needs it is missing from the plan, or it isn’t needed.
health.plan-unused-endpoints.detail.othe: No planned page or service calls them. Either a screen that needs them is missing from the plan, or they aren’t needed.
health.plan-loose-files.title.one: One planned file isn’t connected to anything
health.plan-loose-files.title.other: {n} planned files aren’t connected to anything
health.plan-loose-files.detail.one: Nothing in the plan uses it, and it doesn’t use anything. That usually means a connection is missing from the plan.
health.plan-loose-files.detail.other: Nothing in the plan uses them, and they don’t use anything. That usually means a connection is missing from the plan.
health.plan-loose-files.note: Not connected to anything in the plan

targets.button.title: Where your app writes and reads data, and which parts do it
targets.title: Targets
targets.intro: The databases, services, files and APIs your app writes to or reads from, as listed in floorplan/targets.json. A target with “One writer only” should be written to by exactly one part.

targets.conflicts.other: {n} targets have more than one writer

targets.note.undeclared: Calls {name}, but isn’t listed in targets.json
layers.button.title: Colour the map by layer: the system you could publish, the setup of this installation, and your content
layers.title: Layers
layers.intro: From floorplan/layers.json: which files are the system you could publish, which are the setup of this one installation, and which are your own content. A part takes the layer most of its files have; when none has more than half, it’s mixed.
layers.hint.system: Code and docs anyone could install and run
layers.hint.config: The setup of this one installation: key names, ids, paths, private settings
layers.hint.content: Your own data: customers, amounts, mails
layers.hint.mixed: Parts whose files are spread over more than one layer, none with more than half
layers.switchOn: Switch on Layers in the top bar to colour the map.
ops.button.title: Show what your own tooling reports about the running system: a status dot on each box, with the version and last runs on hover
ops.title: Operations
ops.intro: What your own tooling reports about the running system, from floorplan/ops.json: a status for each part, the version it runs, when it last ran and last ran well, and its last error. Floorplan never writes this file.
ops.stale.label: Stale
ops.stale: This is more than a day old. Check that whatever writes ops.json still runs.
ops.live: Fetched again from the map's server every minute.
ops.switchOn: Switch on Ops in the top bar to show the status dots.
rules.button.title: The rules and decisions the project documents, and where on the map they apply
rules.title: Rules
rules.intro: The rules and dated decisions the project documents, from floorplan/rules.json, each hung on the parts, files, endpoints and targets it applies to, with the place it is written down. Floorplan never makes one up.
clock.button.title: What a clock starts: every schedule found in the code or listed in schedules.json, when it runs and what it runs
clock.title: Clock
clock.intro: What a clock starts, not a person: the schedules the scan found in the code (GitHub Actions, Vercel, n8n, crontabs, ofelia) and the ones listed in floorplan/schedules.json, each with what it triggers and what runs. The strip is one day, with a mark for every start.
clock.counts: {found} found in the code · {declared} from schedules.json
clock.strip: One day, 0 to 24 h, a mark for every start. A plan without a fixed time of day has none.
clock.offHint: Switched off in schedules.json: not on the strip, not on the map.
clock.noTrigger: Nothing is named as the trigger: add "trigger" (a file or a part) in schedules.json.
clock.nothingOnMap: Nothing of it is on the map yet: name the parts it runs under "runs" in schedules.json.
clock.switchOn: Switch on Clock in the top bar to mark the cards a schedule starts.
outcomes.button.title: The map from your side: what arrives on your phone, in your calendar, your database or your inbox, and which flow brings it
outcomes.title: What you see
outcomes.intro: The map from your side, not the code's: for every place something arrives (your phone, your calendar, your database, your inbox), what you see there and which flow brings it. A line opens the flow at that step.

glossary.api.text: The way programs talk to each other: one asks for something (prices, an order) and the other answers.
glossary.endpoint.text: One specific request the app can receive, like "mark this order shipped"; each has its own web address.
glossary.webhook.text: A message another service sends your app automatically when something happens there, like "a payment went through".
glossary.server.text: A computer in the cloud that runs your app's behind-the-scenes work and answers requests from the screens.
glossary.frontend.text: The part of the app people see and click: the screens, buttons and forms in the browser.
glossary.backend.text: The behind-the-scenes part of the app that stores the records, applies the rules and talks to other services.
glossary.database.text: Where the app keeps its records (products, orders, customers) so nothing is lost when it restarts.
glossary.record.text: One saved entry in the database, like a single order or customer; a table is the list of all records of one kind.
glossary.model.text: In code, a model describes how one kind of record (an order, a customer) is stored in the database.
glossary.query.text: A question the app asks the database, like "all orders from today that haven't shipped".
glossary.queue.text: A waiting line of tasks; work is dropped in and handled one by one in the background so nothing gets lost.
glossary.backgroundJob.text: A task that runs on its own behind the scenes, so people don't have to wait for it on screen.
glossary.scheduledJob.text: A task that runs automatically on a timetable, like every hour or every night.
glossary.envVar.text: A setting stored outside the code, such as which database or account to use, so it can differ between test and live.
glossary.secret.text: A password or key the app uses to sign in to another service; it must never be shared or put in the code.
glossary.deploy.text: Putting a new version of the app live so people start using it.
glossary.migration.text: A one-time change to how records are stored, like adding a new field to every order.
glossary.cache.text: A saved copy of something kept close by so it loads faster instead of being worked out again.
glossary.signIn.text: Checking who someone is (usually with a password) before letting them in.
glossary.permissions.text: The rules for who is allowed to do what, like only managers issuing refunds.
glossary.session.text: How the app remembers you are signed in, so you don't have to type your password on every screen.
glossary.token.text: A temporary digital pass the app hands out after sign-in and checks on every request.
glossary.sdk.text: A ready-made kit of code a company provides so apps can talk to its service more easily.
glossary.repository.text: The folder that holds all of a project's code and its full history of changes.
glossary.component.text: A reusable building block of the screens, like a button, a table or a whole product editor.
glossary.route.text: A web address the app answers: on the screens it's a page, on the server it's a kind of request.
glossary.request.text: A message asking the server to do or fetch something; the server sends back a response with the result.
glossary.json.text: A simple text format programs use to send data to each other, like a labelled list.
glossary.rest.text: A common style for building APIs, where each web address stands for a kind of thing (orders, products).
glossary.httpMethod.text: The kind of request: GET reads something, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, DELETE removes.
glossary.http.text: The language browsers and servers use to talk over the web; HTTPS is the encrypted version.
glossary.cdn.text: A network of servers around the world that delivers images and files quickly from somewhere near the visitor.
glossary.bucket.text: Cloud file storage for things like product images, uploads and exports.
glossary.pubSub.text: Google's message service: one part of the app posts an event and others pick it up to handle in the background.
glossary.mcp.text: A standard way to connect AI assistants (like Claude or ChatGPT) to an app so they can look things up in it.
glossary.nextjs.text: A popular toolkit for building websites and web apps with React.
glossary.react.text: A popular library for building interactive screens out of reusable pieces.
glossary.flask.text: A Python toolkit for building web servers.
glossary.sqlalchemy.text: A Python toolkit that lets the code read and save database records without writing raw database commands.
glossary.postgres.text: A widely used database; RDS and Cloud SQL are Amazon's and Google's hosted versions of it.
glossary.docker.text: A way to package an app with everything it needs so it runs the same on any computer or cloud.
glossary.cloudRun.text: Google's service for running an app's servers and background jobs in the cloud without managing machines.
glossary.middleware.text: A check every request passes through on its way in, such as "is this person signed in?".
glossary.blueprint.text: In Flask, a group of related requests bundled together, like all the order requests.
glossary.tests.text: Automatic checks that the code still does what it should, run before changes go live.
glossary.script.text: A small program run by hand for a one-off job, like fixing or importing data.
glossary.oauth.text: The standard behind "Sign in with…" buttons: it lets one app use another on your behalf without sharing your password.
